abstracts.abstract: Understanding human behavior in pervasive environments demands fundamentally new theoretical approaches that transcend conventional context-awareness models. This paper presents Distributed Emergent Context (DEC), a novel theoretical framework that conceptualizes contextual understanding as an emergent property arising from decentralized sensor interactions rather than centralized inference. Unlike conventional approaches relying on predefined context ontologies and centralized processing, DEC establishes three foundational principles: contextual equivalence relations that define context boundaries through distributed consensus mechanisms, emergence operators that characterize how micro-level sensor readings produce macro-level contextual understanding, and stability conditions ensuring contextual coherence across dynamic network topologies. Mathematical proofs demonstrate that under mild network connectivity assumptions, DEC achieves context inference accuracy comparable to centralized approaches while requiring substantially less computational overhead. The proposed formalism offers a new theoretical lens for pervasive computing research, repositioning context-awareness as an emergent rather than engineered phenomenon. This paradigm shift enables systems that naturally adapt to environmental heterogeneity and scale gracefully with network growth, fundamentally reconceptualizing how we approach the design of pervasive computing applications.

Existing probabilistic models for mobile sensing often struggle to balance inference accuracy with computational tractability, particularly when processing high-dimensional sensor data streams in dynamic contexts. This paper presents a significantly improved theoretical framework that advances the state of the art through hierarchical Bayesian inference enhanced with temporal context priors. The hierarchical structure explicitly models sensor correlations across spatial and temporal scales, capturing both immediate readings and longer-term behavioral patterns. This representation enables substantially improved prediction accuracy compared to flat Bayesian models while maintaining computational tractability through novel approximation techniques. Theoretical analysis establishes that inference complexity scales logarithmically with network size, compared to polynomial scaling in existing approaches—a significant improvement enabling sophisticated context-aware applications on resource-constrained mobile devices. The framework provides formal guarantees for dynamic scenarios including network topology changes and sensor failures, maintaining performance guarantees across varying operational conditions. Experimental validation across diverse sensing modalities demonstrates consistent improvements in prediction accuracy ranging from 15% to 35% depending on context complexity, with computational requirements reduced by an order of magnitude compared to existing methods.

The proliferation of IoT devices has created unprecedented opportunities for smart space applications, yet existing architectures fail to address fundamental challenges in real-time responsiveness, privacy preservation, and seamless human-device interaction. This paper presents AmbientFlow, a novel system architecture that fundamentally reimagines how intelligent environments respond to human presence and activity. The architecture introduces distributed edge intelligence, where contextual awareness emerges from collaborative processing across heterogeneous devices rather than relying on cloud-centric processing or isolated device ecosystems. The three-tier processing model—proximate sensors performing initial signal processing, edge nodes executing intermediate inference tasks, and cloud resources handling long-term learning and coordination—enables privacy-sensitive processing by keeping raw sensor data localized while supporting sophisticated ambient intelligence capabilities. Novel mechanisms for dynamic service composition allow applications to automatically assemble functionality across devices based on real-time context and user needs. Implementation and evaluation across diverse environments including smart offices, healthcare facilities, and residential settings demonstrate sub-100ms response times, 95% activity recognition accuracy, and strong privacy preservation. This architecture establishes a new paradigm for smart space development that fundamentally reconceptualizes how intelligent environments support human activities.

Current indoor positioning systems face fundamental limitations in accuracy, energy efficiency, and robustness to environmental variations. This paper presents LocSense, an improved system that significantly advances the state of the art across multiple performance dimensions for location-based services. The system leverages smartphone sensors through an innovative fusion architecture combining Wi-Fi fingerprinting, magnetic field mapping, and motion model predictions using an adaptive weighting scheme rather than static fusion weights. A key innovation involves online learning mechanisms that continuously refine fusion parameters based on environmental characteristics and user movement patterns, substantially improving robustness to environmental dynamics such as furniture repositioning or crowd density variations. The implementation incorporates an energy-aware sampling strategy that reduces sensor polling frequency during stable periods, achieving threefold battery life improvement compared to existing high-accuracy systems. Extensive evaluation across multiple buildings and device types demonstrates median positioning error of 1.2 meters, representing 40% improvement over comparable systems, while maintaining the energy efficiency required for continuous mobile operation. This work demonstrates that adaptive sensor fusion substantially advances the practical deployment of continuous indoor tracking for pervasive computing applications.
